ai-b9d518bf74.fulltext:
The valuation came as the artificial intelligence startup closed on new funding of $11 billion, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters Friday (Nov. 6).
That figure represents just part of OpenAI’s initial goal of $30 billion, while the valuation has fallen from the $1.5 trillion level the company had been seeking, said two investors.
Enthusiasm about AI companies has waned in the last month, the report added, with some investors valuing competing AI startup Anthropic’s planned initial public offering (IPO) at about $1.5 trillion, below earlier expectations of roughly $2 trillion.
An earlier Reuters report cited four sources familiar with Anthropic’s investor discussions said potential backers are skeptical that the company can move ahead with its planned roadshow this week and a November listing.
Even if the company and investors can come to an agreement on a valuation, Anthropic could choose to postpone its IPO until the current market turmoil dies down.
Reuters reported Thursday (Nov. 5) that a selloff that day had wiped out $2.5 trillion in market value from Nasdaq and represented the market’s largest one-day drop since April 2025. The report attributed the decline to investor worries that Democratic victories in last week’s midterm elections could bring more scrutiny for AI-related issues like data center construction.
“Democrats are preparing a slate of artificial intelligence bills for when they take control of Congress in January,” PYMNTS wrote last week.
Among them is Rep. Bill Foster’s, D-Ill., Real-Time Regulatory Study Act, which would direct financial regulators to develop, test and publicly release open-source demonstration software.
“With advances in AI creating new cybersecurity threats and financial risks, it’s more important than ever that we modernize the way we monitor the health of our financial institutions,” Foster said in the release.
And Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., plans to pursue a bill requiring independent experts to test AI models against safety standards, while also clarifying when companies can be held liable for harm their systems cause.
A separate report from Bloomberg News quotes a source who says the rest of the round, which could climb to as much as $20 billion in total, is expected to wrap up in the weeks ahead.

ai-2b527a5d8a.headline: Nvidia opens investigation after report CEO Jensen Huang was target of foreign intelligence
ai-2b527a5d8a.fulltext:
Nvidia said on Sunday it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.
The New York Times reported in October that Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence that Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”
Trump also brushed off a question about whether he now regrets not acting on the intelligence when he was briefed on it, and suggested that he would be happy to take Huang with him on a trip to Asia next week. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody. But, you know, so does everybody else.”
Republican lawmakers have expressed more alarm, asking Huang to give the Houseforeign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his relationship withAlice Huang or Huang Le, an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed, who is of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her.
Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
The company’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.
“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”
Huang fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added.
Axios reported on Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full responsibility for his actions.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did,” Huang said in the draft email also seen by Reuters.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report.
The Times reported on Sunday that a memo drafted by US secretary of state Marco Rubio circulated among top policymakers in the Trump administration last spring, citing intelligence that the businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive was a spy for China’s ministry of state security. Despite those concerns, Huang was invited to join Trump’s delegation when he traveled to China in May. Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, were also invited to a state dinner at the White House in September for Xi Jinping and seated at the top table with Trump and China’s president.
Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom, placing Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
However, national security concerns have prompted strict US export controls, effectively barring the company from selling its top-tier processors to customers in China.
US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as a rationale for the restrictions. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Alice Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.
A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.
Nick Robins-Early and Blake Montgomery contributed reporting

global-economics-c40e022b20.headline: Anthropic secures $3.4 billion generator deal for AI data centers, FT reports
global-economics-c40e022b20.fulltext:
[Text below is Yahoo Finance's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Investing.com -- Anthropic has struck a $3.4 billion deal to secure gas-fired generators for its data centres, deepening its push into the energy industry as AI developers seek greater control over electricity supplies amid soaring demand and equipment shortages.
The Financial Times reported, citing a person familiar with the matter, that the AI company secured commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty generators from San Antonio-based OnePWR Solutions in late September. The transaction also includes engineering and construction capabilities needed to install the equipment.
The deal represents the largest known single purchase of power-generation equipment by an AI laboratory, highlighting how technology companies are increasingly bypassing traditional suppliers to secure electricity infrastructure as manufacturing lead times stretch years into the future.
The generator purchase comes as Anthropic seeks greater control over the infrastructure supporting its AI operations. The company disclosed nearly $900 billion in computing commitments through 2045, having relied heavily on partners to secure power, chips, data centres and land.
OnePWR had ordered the generators from Caterpillar about two years ago but needed financing to complete the transaction. Anthropic had initially planned to become a OnePWR customer before opting to take over the existing equipment orders, the report said.
Anthropic did not acquire OnePWR itself, and none of the supplier's employees transferred to the AI company, according to the Financial Times.
The move follows similar efforts by technology companies to secure power-generation capacity directly. SpaceX's AI subsidiary xAI bought mobile gas turbines for $2 billion earlier this year, while Google's parent Alphabet acquired energy developer Intersect in late 2025.
Anthropic is also a major SpaceX customer, with its monthly payments to lease computing capacity expected to reach $3.1 billion by year-end, according to the Financial Times.
Anthropic is preparing for a potential initial public offering as early as November, which could rank among the largest listings in history. However, its ambitious infrastructure spending plans face financing challenges, with Blackstone warning investors that the company might receive a junk credit rating rather than the investment-grade rating previously expected.

work-careers-49f98482d8.headline: Hiring is up 14 per cent. Software engineering hiring is up 1.
work-careers-49f98482d8.fulltext:
India's white-collar hiring rose 14 per cent in October 2026, according to the Naukri JobSpeak Index. Automobile hiring rose 36 per cent and AI and machine learning roles 32 per cent. Hiring for software engineering and quality assurance, the work that built India's IT middle class, rose 1 per cent.
What did October's hiring data show?
White-collar hiring rose 14 per cent on a year earlier. The Naukri JobSpeak Index, which tracks new job postings and recruiter searches on Naukri.com, stood at 2,836 in October 2026 against 2,480 in October 2025.
Two cautions apply. Naukri itself noted that Diwali fell in October 2025, which depressed last year's base and flatters this year's comparison. And the index actually fell from 3,053 in September. The rise is annual, not monthly. September's year-on-year growth was 2 per cent.
Where is the growth?
In production, automobiles and specialist technology. Production and manufacturing roles, a job function measured across all industries, rose 39 per cent. The automobile industry rose 36 per cent, and within it research and development hiring rose 53 per cent. AI and machine learning roles rose 32 per cent, and hiring by global capability centres 18 per cent. BPO and IT-enabled services rose 17 per cent, and banking and financial services 16 per cent.
Where is it standing still?
In general software. Hiring in the IT and software services industry rose 5 per cent. Software engineering and quality assurance roles, measured across all industries, rose 1 per cent.
These are the roles that turned Indian IT into the country's largest creator of salaried professional jobs. They are also the roles generative AI is best placed to draft, test and document. A separate ICRIER survey of 651 IT firms found close to two-thirds classing software developers and application developers as significantly exposed to AI.
Who is being hired?
Experience is being paid for. Fresher hiring rose 15 per cent. Hiring for professionals with 13 to 16 years of experience, and for those with more than 16, rose 22 per cent each. Among the metros, Hyderabad led at 15 per cent, followed by Pune at 14 per cent and Delhi-NCR at 13 per cent. Kolkata was flat.
What should a professional read into this?
That the headline is an average of two markets moving at different speeds. One is hiring for specialist skills in AI, data, engineering and production. The other, general software delivery, is barely moving. A software engineer reading '14 per cent' as good news for their own search is reading the wrong row.
The November index, due in early December, will be the first clean comparison without a festive distortion. Signals will track it.
Sources

- Naukri JobSpeak, October 2026, reported by SightsIn Plus, 3 November 2026

ai-8f97d22ce6.headline: Global AI sell-off turns into India's gain as FPIs pump ₹46,000 crore in 5 sessions; will the buying spree sustain?
ai-8f97d22ce6.fulltext:
A KsheerasagarPublished8 Nov 2026, 05:01 PM IST It appears that foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have changed their bearish stance towards the Indian stock market, buying domestic equities aggressively last week and pouring in a massive ₹45,970 crore in just five trading sessions. This marks a strong turnaround after foreign investors remained net sellers for two consecutive months. The shift in sentiment boosted the Nifty 50 by 8.6% during the week, marking its strongest weekly performance since February 2021. The rally also helped the index pare its year-to-date losses to 4.21%. At its lowest point this year, the index had fallen nearly 15% but has since recovered close to 13% from its yearly low. In addition to equities, the inflows have also strengthened the Indian rupee, which had suffered multiple record lows this year. The currency climbed 0.6% to 93.91 against the US dollar, its strongest level since April. The shift in sentiment towards Asia's third-largest economy comes amid a correction in global AI-linked stocks. Concerns over a potential move by the US Congress, led by Democrats, to impose restrictions on the massive expansion of data centres in the US triggered a sell-off in previously favoured chip and memory stocks across Asia. In addition, the sharp retreat in crude oil prices has eased inflation concerns, particularly as India remains heavily dependent on oil imports. An improving earnings outlook has further enhanced the appeal of Indian equities among foreign investors. India's relatively low exposure to the AI trade had previously left its stocks among Asia's worst performers. However, as the once high-flying trade begins to unravel, that weakness has quickly turned into an advantage. Dheeraj Gaur, Chief Investment Strategy Officer at Choice Wealth, said three factors came together to drive the sharp rally in Indian equities. First, politics and oil: the US midterm results were read as raising the odds of a de-escalation in the US–Iran conflict, and Brent fell about 13% to roughly $98 – its steepest weekly drop since the start of Covid. Cheaper oil is the single biggest relief for India’s inflation, current account and rupee, and the rupee strengthened to about 93.90 per dollar from around 95.4 a week ago. Second, the AI trade cracked. A tech rout on Thursday took the Nasdaq down 5.5% and the S&P 500 4.4%, after weak Qualcomm results and worries about slowing AI infrastructure spending, and Korea and Japan fell about 6% on Friday. Global funds have been rotating out of AI-linked names into markets like India, which has little AI exposure – Indian IT stocks even rose. Third, India simply looked cheap after a poor year, with earnings holding up. Looking ahead, Dheeraj Gaur, said several factors will determine the direction of FPI flows. The US Consumer Price Index (CPI) data due on Tuesday, November 10, will be closely watched. With a December rate hike nearly priced in, a hotter-than-expected inflation reading could push bond yields and the US dollar higher. Gaur also highlighted crude oil prices and developments in the Gulf region as key factors to watch, particularly whether Brent crude sustains below the $100-a-barrel mark or the de-escalation narrative begins to lose momentum. In addition, commentary from Federal Reserve officials and movements in US bond yields will be closely monitored following the latest jobs report, as any hawkish messaging around a December rate hike could influence global fund flows. climate-energy-69547e43ae.headline: Rs 14,500 Crore push to power India round the clock, targets 92GWh grid energy storage
climate-energy-69547e43ae.fulltext:
The Union Cabinet has cleared a Rs 14,500 crore Viability Gap Funding scheme to build 92 GWh of grid-scale energy storage by 2030-31. Its 40 per cent domestic content rule neatly links clean power, grid stability and Atmanirbhar battery manufacturing.
The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on November 4, approved a Viability Gap Funding (VGF) Scheme worth Rs 14,500 crore for grid-scale energy storage. The scheme will back 92 GWh of new storage capacity between FY 2026-27 and FY 2030-31. It is expected to draw a total investment of Rs 97,600 crore.
The new capacity equals 170 per cent of India’s present grid-scale storage base. In plain terms, the country plans to build in five years nearly twice what it has today. Every rupee of public support is expected to pull in close to seven rupees of overall investment.
India’s clean energy story has moved faster than many predicted. Non-fossil capacity reached 300.5 GW on July 31, 2026, with solar alone contributing 164.59 GW. These sources now make up more than 54 per cent of the country’s installed capacity of around 552 GW. In FY 2025-26, India added a record 55.29 GW of such capacity.
This success brings its own challenge. The sun sets every evening, and the wind does not blow on demand. India’s peak demand often arrives after dark, when solar output falls to zero. Without storage, surplus daytime power goes to waste, and the evening shortfall is met by coal. Storage closes this gap. It captures cheap solar power at noon and releases it during the evening peak. It also helps grid operators handle sudden swings in supply and keeps frequency stable. That is why the Central Electricity Authority estimates that India will need about 411 GWh of grid-scale storage by 2031-32.
The 92 GWh will come from three sources. The largest share, 60 GWh, will come from hydro pumped storage plants (PSPs). Another 30 GWh will come from battery energy storage systems (BESS). The remaining 2 GWh is reserved for emerging storage technologies.
Pumped storage works like a giant water battery. Surplus solar power runs pumps that lift water to an upper reservoir. When demand rises, the water flows down through turbines and generates electricity. Such plants last for decades and suit long-duration needs. Batteries play a different role. They respond in milliseconds, can be installed quickly and fit close to solar parks or substations. The small window for new technologies keeps the door open for flow batteries, compressed air or thermal storage. India will not be locked into a single path as technology evolves.
Capacity under the scheme will be allocated through tariff-based competitive bidding. Public and private electricity distribution companies will be eligible for VGF on BESS and pumped storage projects. Projects using alternative technologies will be implemented by public and private sector entities.
Placing discoms at the centre is a sensible choice. They buy the power and face the evening peak. Linking support to bids ensures that public money goes to the most efficient developers. It also keeps the final cost of stored power low for consumers.
The new scheme builds on two earlier rounds that have already delivered. In September 2023, the Cabinet approved an Rs 3,760 crore VGF for 4 GWh of batteries. As battery prices fell, the supported capacity was expanded to about 13.2 GWh within the same outlay. In June 2025, the Ministry of Power launched a second VGF of Rs 5,400 crore for 30 GWh of BESS. It was funded through the Power System Development Fund. Of this capacity, 25 GWh went to 15 states and 5 GWh to NTPC. The results show tariffs. Battery storage discovered through bidding cost about Rs 10.18 per kWh in 2022-23. By December 2025, the government reported that this had fallen to around Rs 2.1 per kWh without VGF, assuming two cycles a day. Few sectors have seen such a sharp fall in so short a time.
The Centre has also waived interstate transmission charges in full for BESS co-located with renewable plants and commissioned by June 30, 2028. Together, these steps have turned storage from a costly experiment into a bankable asset.
The most significant feature of the new scheme is its focus on self-reliance. All BESS projects must meet a minimum Domestic Content Requirement (DCR) of 40 per cent. This rule creates assured demand for Indian-made cells, packs, inverters and control systems. It also completes a policy loop. On the supply side, the Production Linked Incentive scheme for Advanced Chemistry Cell batteries carries an outlay of Rs 18,100 crore. It targets 50 GWh of domestic cell manufacturing, with 10 GWh earmarked for grid-scale use. The VGF now supplies the demand that such factories need to scale up.
The same Cabinet meeting cleared a Rs 2,814 crore scheme to support domestic processing of critical minerals such as lithium and nickel. Read together, the two decisions trace a full value chain. It runs from minerals to cells to grid-connected storage. This is Atmanirbhar Bharat in practical form. India learnt a lesson from its solar journey. When module manufacturing lagged behind installations, imports filled the gap. The DCR clause ensures that storage does not repeat that pattern.
For households, the benefit is reliable and affordable power through day and night. Fewer evening shortages mean fewer outages. Discoms will also rely less on costly peak-hour purchases from the exchange. Over time, this should ease pressure on tariffs.
For industry, the scheme opens a large and assured market. The projected investment will flow into civil works, turbines, batteries and grid equipment. Pumped storage projects will create jobs in hilly and remote regions. Battery manufacturing will build skills in a sector the world is racing to lead.
For the nation, the gains go beyond economics. Storage reduces the need to burn fossil fuels for balancing power. It strengthens energy security and supports India’s goal of 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030. It also moves the country closer to its net-zero commitment for 2070.
Execution will decide success. Pumped storage projects need careful site selection, environmental clearances and long construction periods. Battery projects must meet the 40 per cent DCR even as domestic cell capacity is still being built. Timely bidding and steady discom participation will be vital.
The scheme recognises that the next phase of India’s energy transition is not about adding more panels alone. It is about making clean power available whenever the nation needs it. With storage as its backbone, the grid of Viksit Bharat can run on the sun long after sunset.

climate-energy-d98f8d274a.headline: Hyperscalers favour southern wind-solar hybrids over Kutch and Rajasthan
climate-energy-d98f8d274a.fulltext:
Global technology companies buying renewable power in India are increasingly choosing wind-solar hybrid projects in the south over those in Kutch and Rajasthan, according to CleanMax Enviro Energy Solutions Ltd. Management said on its second quarter (Q2) FY27 earnings call on 4 November that buyers are wary of curtailment risk in the western and northern regions.
Founder and Managing Director Kuldeep Jain said hyperscaler customers want projects connected to the central transmission utility (CTU) network. They also prefer wind-solar hybrids to solar alone, because a combined profile matches their demand better through the day and across the year.
Jain gave two reasons for the tilt towards South India. Buyers perceive a curtailment risk in Kutch and Rajasthan, and many hyperscalers are setting up their own data centres in the south.
CleanMax said all its CTU-connected capacity through September 2028 is already sold. It has applied for more CTU connectivity to replenish its stock, including another 2 GW since 30 September.
The company has reserved its limited CTU capacity for hyperscalers rather than offering it to group captive customers such as smelters, even though those customers have approached it. Jain said demand from hyperscalers for CTU-based projects is high enough that CleanMax made this a deliberate business decision.
Hyperscalers account for roughly 27-28% of CleanMax’s 6.2 GW of contracted capacity. Jain said the company holds about 35% of the hyperscaler energy volumes contracted in India so far. He added that CleanMax has multiple deals over several years with each hyperscaler, so the share does not depend on one or two relationships.
According to Jain, hyperscalers want sole discretion to either feed the power directly into a data centre or use it only for green attributes, as they keep expanding and have energy offset requirements. He said CleanMax gets the same tariffs locked in for 20-25 years either way, so it is indifferent to how the customer uses the power.
CleanMax has faced grid curtailment itself. Its Bikaner plant saw curtailment of about 70% in the first quarter, nearly 50% in July and August, and 44% after that. The figure fell to 26% in October as the grid added capacity. Management said curtailment cost about 5% of first-half earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA).
Jain said hyperscaler contracts are large and bulky, with typically no more than one announcement a year, so the company does not give guidance on when they will be signed. He said conversations with hyperscalers and colocation data centres are at a record high.
Asked about a deal combining wind, solar and storage for a data centre, he said none has been signed yet. CleanMax will disclose material agreements as required by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) rules, he added.

climate-energy-7d732f8c42.headline: India's clean energy push cut its fuel import bill by $240 billion: IEA
climate-energy-7d732f8c42.fulltext:
India's shift towards renewable energy could help it save billions on fuel imports, while making the country less dependent on global energy markets.
The transition could bring cumulative savings of nearly $240 billion on coal and natural gas imports by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).
As India expands its clean energy capacity, the benefits are going beyond sustainability. The move is also strengthening the country's energy security and economic resilience. IEA executive director Fatih Birol said India's experience could offer useful lessons for other emerging economies looking to expand renewable energy.
Consistent policies helping India attract clean energy investments
In a post on X, Birol said India's renewable energy expansion was helping the country deal with uncertainty in global energy markets by reducing its dependence on imported fossil fuels.
"India’s renewables expansion is delivering major energy security benefits amid heightened uncertainty in global energy markets," Birol said.
He added that India's experience demonstrated "how consistent policies can help drive down renewable energy costs and attract investment, offering valuable lessons for other emerging economies".
Birol was responding to a post by Union minister for new and renewable energy Prahlad Joshi, who highlighted the economic benefits of India's renewable energy transition.
Joshi said the shift was not just about making energy cleaner. It was also strengthening India's energy security and economic resilience by reducing import dependence and conserving foreign exchange.
India could save $240 billion on coal and gas imports by 2030
The minister shared an report on the IEA's India Renewable Energy Market Report 2026, which estimated that India's cumulative savings on coal and natural gas imports could approach $240 billion by 2030.
This projection assumes that fuel prices remain broadly in line with their 2024-25 averages.
The savings are also expected to make a significant difference to India's annual import bill. The report projected that annual savings on fossil fuel imports could reach around $35 billion by 2030. This would be higher than the country's actual non-coking coal and natural gas import bill in FY 2024-25.
Solar and wind power are expected to account for most of these savings. Solar photovoltaic power could contribute nearly 60 per cent of the projected cumulative savings, while wind power could account for almost 30 per cent.
Solar to lead renewable energy expansion
India's renewable energy capacity could reach around 530 GW by 2030, according to the IEA's projections. Solar power is expected to drive much of this growth, with its capacity projected to exceed 350 GW.
However, generating more renewable electricity is only part of the task. The agency has highlighted the need for continued investment in transmission infrastructure, energy storage and power system flexibility to accommodate the growing share of renewable electricity.
Birol's remarks highlight how India's clean energy expansion is helping strengthen energy security while offering the possibility of substantial savings on fuel imports. The country's experience with consistent policies, lower renewable energy costs and investment could also provide useful lessons for other emerging economies.

agritech-4b831b3cc8.headline: Warmer oceans, fewer monsoon depressions: Study reveals why India’s rainfall is shifting south
agritech-4b831b3cc8.fulltext:
Dehradun: Warmer oceans across the Indo-Pacific region may be weakening the weather systems that bring rain to large parts of India, a new study has found.
The number of monsoon depressions over Bay of Bengal fell from 26 in the 1980s to 10 between 2010 and 2020, with the sharpest decline in August, when their formation usually peaks. The change has also shifted rainfall away from parts of eastern and central India towards the southern peninsula, researchers said.
Monsoon depressions are low-pressure weather systems that usually form over Bay of Bengal and move inland. They bring widespread rain over several days and contribute significantly to the June-Sept monsoon, particularly across eastern, central and northern India.
The study, published in Journal of Earth System Science late Oct, analysed 40 years of weather data, from 1980 to 2020, to understand why these systems have become less frequent despite rising sea surface temperatures.
Warmer oceans generally provide more moisture and energy for weather systems, but researchers said the pattern of warming across the Indo-Pacific has made conditions less favourable for depressions to form over the Bay of Bengal.
The equatorial Indian Ocean and western Pacific have warmed more than the northern Bay of Bengal. This difference has weakened two large-scale atmospheric circulation systems, known as Walker and Hadley circulations, which help move heat and moisture around the planet. 
As a result, fewer winds converge over Bay of Bengal and less moist air rises from the surface, reducing the chances of monsoon depressions forming.
The researchers identified weaker cyclonic circulation near the ocean surface as the main reason for the decline. Although the atmosphere has more moisture and energy, these factors have not been enough to offset the weakening of the weather systems.
The researchers also found that rainfall has declined along the usual paths of monsoon depressions, particularly over 
Odisha
, central India and the Gangetic plains. In contrast, parts of peninsular India have received more rain, suggesting a shift in rainfall distribution rather than a uniform decline across the country.
The changes could affect agriculture, groundwater recharge and water supplies in regions that depend heavily on these weather systems, the researchers said.
The study was conducted by researchers associated with Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), Pune, Jawaharlal Nehru University and Central University of Haryana.

indian-startups-0cfd12f59b.headline: Profits Are Just Half The Story This Earnings Season
indian-startups-0cfd12f59b.fulltext: The 2026 festive season began in muted fashion, but the performance of some of the key new-age tech stocks in the pre-festive quarter (Q2 FY27) shows that even in this environment businesses are able to extract and expand profits, and grow their topline. When we see the financial performance of ecommerce, fintech and logistics stocks, it’s clear companies entered this period with a lot more confidence and absorbed some of these headwinds. Pretty much each one of them improved on their profitability metrics and their topline. As Inc42 reported in October, early data from the festive season sales indicated that Indian consumers kept shopping, but with more abandon. Online sales slipped from last year, card spending and smartphone sales weakened, and surveys suggest urban households are trimming discretionary budgets too. Rising household costs, uncertainty over jobs and incomes, and discounts that no longer feel compelling have made shoppers wary of big-ticket purchases. Consumers are still browsing for products, but in the current climate, conversion rates have fallen for premium products, which usually see a big uptick. A lot of this has to do with the macroeconomic factors, rising energy prices and logistics costs, and lingering grave geopolitical concerns that have dented consumer confidence and spending. In Q2, logistics tech players expanded capacity ahead of the festive shopping rush, with higher volumes offering an opportunity to improve operating leverage. Ecommerce companies capitalised on seasonal demand, even as the pressure to balance growth with profitability persisted. Meanwhile, fintech companies, particularly those with a big UPI focus, faced a different equation: the prospect of merchant discount rates (MDR) on select UPI transactions. While MDR itself is yet to come into effect, the fintech ecosystem’s quarter was defined by swelling toplines, which bodes well for the next quarter where MDR is likely to become a real factor. Profitability broadened across the listed new-age tech universe, with nine of the 11 large tech stocks (with a market cap of over ₹10,000 Cr) across these key sectors reporting a net profit in Q2 FY27. The combined bottomline of these companies improved by around ₹1,100–1,400 Cr year-on-year (YoY), depending on how exceptional items in the base quarter are treated, according to market data. More importantly, EBITDA grew faster than revenue at all nine profitable companies, suggesting that operating leverage is beginning to show up in reported performance. But a significant profit pool remained concentrated in a handful of companies, while businesses such as Swiggy and Meesho continue to report losses despite improving operating metrics. Atul Thakkar, executive director at Anand Rathi Investment Banking, believes the market is moving towards rewarding earnings delivery rather than growth narratives. “Over the next 12–18 months, we expect earnings delivery, rather than growth narratives, to be the main driver of returns in this space,” he said, This distinction is particularly relevant when the three major segments, fintech, logistics and ecommerce are assessed separately. Fintech has delivered the strongest operating performance, logistics has shown some of the clearest margin improvement, and ecommerce has produced a wide range of outcomes. But how did the profitability story unfolded across these three sectors? Logistics Tech Shifts Into High Gear It was largely a capacity-building quarter for logistics companies, with the full benefit of festive demand expected to play out in Q3. Yet, the results already point to improving operating leverage, as shipment volumes grew faster than revenue at the larger third-party logistics (3PL) players. Shadowfax’s revenue rose 57%, while express and hyperlocal orders grew nearly 70%. Adjusted EBITDA increased sharply, with margins expanding to 5%. Delhivery reported a similar divergence: express shipments grew 32%, against 22% growth in express revenue. Its adjusted EBITDA margin also improved, while first-half operating cash flow more than doubled. The gap between volume and revenue growth suggests that incremental shipments are not translating into proportionate revenue. Profitability, therefore, will depend on whether higher volumes can offset pricing pressure and rising costs across fuel, wages and last-mile delivery. Delhivery’s return to profitability also needs context: the year-ago quarter included acquisition-related integration costs linked to Ecom Express. Its adjusted EBITDA and cash generation offer a more useful measure of underlying progress. Shiprocket, meanwhile, turned profitable, reporting a net profit of ₹60 Lakh against a loss of ₹20.3 Cr a year ago. Revenue grew 35%, while adjusted EBITDA more than tripled. Its core business continued to expand, with transactions growing 31% and adjusted EBITDA margin improving to 12.8%. The results point to improving economics, although the reported profit remains modest. Across the sector, technology and network utilisation are central to the margin story. Shadowfax is deploying AI-led route optimisation and expanding its seller platform, while Delhivery is investing in automation and autonomous material-handling systems. These initiatives could improve productivity, but their returns will depend on execution and the ability to absorb peak-season volumes without adding costs at the same pace. The festive quarter will be the real test. Stronger volumes should support operating leverage, but sustained margin expansion will require better network utilisation, disciplined pricing and control over fulfilment costs. Logistics is showing clearer signs of improving economics, though the gap between shipment growth and revenue realisation remains a key risk. Fintech’s Profit Engines Roar Fintech was the strongest performer in Q2 FY27, with all the major companies in the segment reporting profits. Moreover, EBITDA growth outpaced revenue growth at each, pointing to improving operating leverage. The gains, however, are coming from deeper monetisation of existing customers rather than payment volumes alone. Paytm is increasingly diversifying beyond payments, with financial services distribution contributing about a third of its revenue. Its merchant subscription base and financial services business continue to expand, reducing its dependence on payment processing. Meanwhile, Pine Labs is extracting more value from its merchant network through subscriptions, affordability products and transaction-linked services. PB Fintech’s growing renewal book offers a similar advantage: recurring insurance revenue is expanding faster than its core insurance business, making growth less dependent on fresh policy acquisition. The bigger question for fintech is whether these operating gains can withstand regulatory changes. The proposed UPI MDR framework could create an additional revenue stream, but the benefit to payment companies will depend on how the pool is shared between banks and other ecosystem participants. With implementation postponed beyond the festive period, it remains an opportunity rather than an earnings driver for now. Insurance distribution faces a more direct overhang. The proposed changes to commission structures and expense limits could alter the economics of online intermediaries such as PB Fintech. Its growing renewal revenue offers some cushion, but the impact on new-policy distribution remains uncertain. “While fintech companies have demonstrated an ability to improve monetisation and operating leverage, the regulatory environment remains a key determinant of how sustainable these gains will be. For this segment, regulation is a bigger variable than execution,” said Thakkar. Ecommerce’s Profitability Divide Widens Ecommerce delivered the widest divergence in Q2 FY27. While revenue growth remained strong across quick commerce, ecommerce and consumer brands, profitability varied sharply, reflecting differences in scale, cost structures and monetisation. For example, Meesho saw its net loss narrow to 68%, while marketplace contribution margin improved to 6% of NMV from 3.3% a year ago. However, newer initiatives remain loss-making and are yet to establish meaningful scale. Consumer brands delivered a more consistent earnings performance. Nykaa’s profit more than tripled, supported by margin expansion and growth across beauty and fashion. Lenskart also reported strong profit growth, with expansion across its India and international businesses. Higher store productivity, rising volumes and operating cash flow suggest that growth is being supported by better utilisation of the existing network, alongside store additions. Input-cost inflation remains another pressure point for consumer brands. Passing on higher costs through pricing could protect margins but risks weighing on demand and average order values. Gross margins, customer retention and acquisition costs will be as important as revenue growth in assessing the durability of earnings. Why Profits Are Just Half The Story As these sectors continue to mature, operating leverage is becoming more important than headline growth. However, profitability remains concentrated, with a handful of companies accounting for a substantial share of the sector’s earnings. The ownership shift is also worth watching. Foreign investors have reduced exposure to several listed new-age tech companies, while domestic institutions have increased participation. But domestic ownership is no guarantee against corrections when earnings or regulatory developments disappoint. According to market analysts, retail investors are likely to increasingly favour companies that are not only profitable but also generate revenue from multiple products within their existing customer base and use operating cash flow to fund expansion. We can see this in the aggressive diversification across the industry, particularly in fintech and logistics tech. This wave favours established fintech businesses, asset-light logistics networks and ecommerce companies where the seller-customer flywheel is up and running. Post the festive season spike, even if it may be a relatively smaller spike compared to previous years, the cash generation and regulatory resilience of these companies will be worth watching. That could very well mark the next phase of maturity. MARKETS WATCH: NEW ISSUES, POST-IPO JOURNEY & MORE Inside Razorpay’s ₹6,000 Cr IPO: As Razorpay gears up for its ₹6,000 Cr IPO, the proposed UPI merchant discount rate and its AI ambitions could shape its valuation. But can these growth levers convince public market investors to look beyond its thin margins? Honasa’s Profit Up 87%: The Mamaearth parent reported an 87% YoY jump in Q2 FY27 net profit to ₹73.2 Cr, while revenue rose 36% to ₹731.2 Cr. Growth across focus categories, offline channels and younger brands helped drive the company’s quarterly performance. Go Digit PAT Dips: Go Digit’s net profit declined 31.1% YoY to ₹142.4 Cr in Q2 FY27 despite a marginal 1.7% rise in insurance revenue to ₹2,720.5 Cr. Higher insurance service expenses and claims weighed on profitability, even as motor insurance revenue grew. RateGain Profit Rises 47%:The travel-focused SaaS company’s profit rose 46.5% YoY to ₹74.7 Cr in Q2 FY27, driven by operating revenue zooming 152.6% YoY to ₹745.4 Cr. This came on the back of the consolidation of travel marketing platform Sojern, which RateGain acquired for $250 Mn last year. Moneyview Revenue Grows 41%: The fintech company’s consolidated net profit surged 417.6% YoY to ₹200.7 Cr in Q2 FY27, while operating revenue grew 41% to ₹1,120.2 Cr. The fintech reported a managed AUM of ₹23,892 Cr, with its shares gaining 5.7% following the earnings announcement.

indian-startups-a29d97177e.headline: Pronto’s Second Shift
indian-startups-a29d97177e.fulltext: Anjali Sardana and Pronto entered India’s domestic services market in 2025 to solve a familiar urban problem: finding reliable house help on demand. The result was a quick commerce-style home services platform, combining technology-led recruitment, standardised training and a hyperlocal network of professionals. Pronto, which competes with Snabbit and Urban Company, says it has served more than half a million households across 11 cities. But the real story of Pronto is being developed far away from the homes and houses that its professionals visit. This is being built in Silicon Valley. Footage recorded by professionals working in thousands of homes every day is helping shape the next generation of robots. The first signs of this ambition emerged in May 2026, when Pronto was reported to be exploring ways to generate physical AI training data using footage captured during household chores. And since then Sardana and Pronto’s ambitions have solidified. In July, Pronto formalised the experiment through Verified, an opt-in premium service in which housekeepers and cleaners wear head-mounted or body-mounted cameras during visits. In October 2026, Sardana set up Provision Labs, a physical AI venture based in San Francisco, which will collect data to train and test AI systems designed to perform real-world tasks using robots and other machines. It will work with developers building physical AI models. A few days later, Provision Labs announced that it is acquiring Mumbai-based Basilisk Industries, a 2023-founded company focused on perception technologies, which help machines interpret their surroundings. Basilisk founder Shourya Watwani will lead Provision’s hardware efforts and work on its in-house post-processing models. Watwani and his team are said to have developed a 3D hand-tracking model and built the first version of a lightweight tactile glove to capture touch-related data. Given this timeline, the fact that Pronto doubled-down on its experiment after the May 2026 introduction does not seem surprising at all. The relationship between Pronto’s household data collection and Provision Labs’ operations, however, remains unclear. Inc42 asked Pronto how the two businesses work together, if at all, but the company declined to comment. The unanswered question is significant: could a network originally built to deliver household services become an acquisition channel for the data needed to train global robotics systems? Why Record Workers? The first reports around Pronto’s collection of worker data triggered a backlash over surveillance and privacy of house help professionals. To assuage some of the critics, Pronto said that customers are informed about the terms several times before recording begins, while personally identifiable information is automatically blurred or removed on the device. “The raw footage is deleted immediately after the work is done, and no one ever accesses it. For 48 hours, an anonymised, end-to-end encrypted recording is available only to the customer, who can watch it in the app to check the work. After that, we use the anonymised footage for AI training, as our terms set out,” the company told Inc42. Pronto said more than half of the professionals participating in Verified already earn over ₹40,000 a month. The company claims workers feel safer knowing there is a record of their work, but no independent studies have been conducted to validate these claims. What’s the point of all this? Unlike chatbots, which can learn from the enormous repositories of text and images available online, physical AI systems need to understand how the real world works. A robot must learn how to pick up objects, fold clothes, navigate a room, and respond when something does not go as expected. This requires large volumes of real-world, multimodal data capturing movement, spatial information and interactions with objects. Such data is considerably harder and more expensive to collect than internet-sourced text and images. ANI quoted a Goldman Sachs report estimating that general-purpose robots could require around 10 Mn hours of high-quality physical interaction data to reach production-level capabilities. The Missing Data Layer One can see the physical AI stack through four layers. The data layer captures real-world interactions, while the model layer uses this information to train vision-language-action models that translate what a robot sees into actions. The simulation layer through platforms such as NVIDIA’s Isaac Sim allow these models to be tested in virtual environments before deployment. Finally, the edge layer runs them on physical robots, with real-world feedback informing and enhancing the training process. Global technology companies such as NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, Amazon, OpenAI and Anthropic are building capabilities across the model and simulation layers of physical AI. India has some representation at the robotics and deployment end, with companies such as Addverb, CynLr and Perceptyne developing robotic systems and automation technologies. But it is the data layer that is seeing a growing crop of Indian startups, alongside global data companies building collection operations that rely heavily on India’s workforce and physical environments. Humyn Labs, EgoData, Egolab.ai, Neocambrian AI, Human Archive, and Objectways have deployed people on the ground to collect footage across household chores, but several are also working with manufacturing units and other industrial environments. Head-mounted or body-mounted cameras and sensor-equipped gloves or even full body suits have become commonplace as the next phase of robotics takes shape. For India, the opportunity has echoes of its earlier role in the AI supply chain. Over the past decade, India has become a hub for data annotation, with workers labelling images, text and audio used to train AI models. Physical AI takes that outsourcing model a step further. Indian workers’ movements, workplaces and interactions with objects are becoming the training material. Abhinav Kukreja, founder of Neocambrian AI, sees India’s large and diverse physical environments as an advantage over markets such as the US, where access to comparable real-world data is more limited. He believes the next phase of robotics will see an explosion of different embodiments and form factors. For India to participate meaningfully in this transition, it needs to control an important part of the underlying ecosystem. “I strongly felt that this layer would not be compute, architecture or algorithms, but the data layer,” he said. Y Combinator-backed Human Archive is pursuing a similar opportunity, with a model that involves home service workers, cooks, cleaners and domestic help wearing cameras inside homes and private properties. Cofounder Rushil Agarwal told Inc42 earlier that the Indian market’s appeal lies in the diversity of industries accessible within the geographical boundary and the large labour pool. This is difficult to replicate in the US. Notably, Human Archive was evaluated by Snabbit too as it looked to launch a Pronto-like data collection pilot. However, the home services company eventually dropped the proposal. Human Archive raised $8.2 Mn in a seed round led by Wing Venture Capital and NVP Capital. Pronto’s $45 Mn Series B also saw participation from Lachy Groom, cofounder of robotics model startup Physical Intelligence; Groom has also backed Provision Labs. Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs, led by former Nazara CEO Manish Agarwal, has committed $20 Mn towards expanding its data collection network. The supply side, meanwhile, is becoming more competitive. Data collection rates fell 30% between January and June this year, an industry executive told Inc42 earlier. More suppliers have since entered the market and synthetic data generation has improved rapidly. But in the long run, the demand for human-captured footage could shrink as physical AI models mature. The larger question is who captures the value and what happens to the workers. We’ll come to the latter soon, but the current situation does not give us any clarity on what this segment might look like in a few months. While Pronto says more than half of its Verified professionals earn over ₹40,000 a month, Human Archive has cited compensation in the range of $1-10 per hour for its data collection work. These disparate compensation structures highlight the lack of clarity on the economic model. One cannot draw parallels between the kind of data captured either till the industry further matures. At this point, companies are throwing a lot more money than they are willing to to attract workers who will readily collect data that can in a few years replace them. Indian manufacturers and industrial units may recruit workers, deploy cameras and collect footage, while the resulting models and intellectual property are developed and owned elsewhere. This value drain could have serious consequences on the Indian economy and the jobs landscape. For data suppliers, the challenge will be moving beyond one-off collection contracts to building differentiated datasets that command lasting value. As more and more companies come into the picture, the collection of egocentric data and first-person footage is about to become highly commodified and consumerised. The Elephant In The Room: What About The Workers? Like we mentioned, the business opportunity comes with a difficult labour question. The blunt reading of the matter is that Indian workers are training the robots that could eventually replace them. Videos circulating on social media have raised concerns about whether workers even understand why they are wearing cameras. Some workers have reported discomfort from prolonged use, which may stretch to 5-10 hours a workday, while others believe the devices are intended to monitor their productivity. Every company maintains that workers are informed about what is being captured and why. However, when collection happens through partner businesses, the responsibility for communicating this information shifts to those partners. An openDemocracy investigation, meanwhile, found that workers at two Delhi factories were asked to wear cameras supplied by Egolab.ai without being told their purpose. Such incidents raise questions about informed consent, compensation, the privacy of other people captured in recordings and ownership of the resulting data. India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, whose implementation is scheduled for May 2027, adds another layer of regulatory uncertainty. Speculation is that the government may regulate these services, but to what extent can it stop individuals from participating is unclear. For Sardana and Pronto, the opportunity is significantly larger than just a quick home services platform. The data from the broad range of everyday human activity by Pronto workers can fuel Provision Labs and Basilisk’s next big plays and turn them into even bigger companies than Pronto. Whether Pronto and Provision Labs will eventually work together has not been answered. But the value of Pronto’s network may very soon be the footage of what its professionals do, rather than the quality of the service itself.

india-deep-tech-c65e8e438e.headline: US ally’s startup wins place in NATO counter-drone framework, boosts key weapon availability
india-deep-tech-c65e8e438e.fulltext:
A French startup, Alta Ares, entered the North Atlantic Treaty Organization’s (NATO) counter-drone framework agreement.
The development, revealed on November 5, allows the allied partner countries to procure protective systems against aerial threats directly from the French defense manufacturer without the need for new tenders.
The company secured 16 awarded lots under the contract, bagging the highest number of awards among the five companies covered under the NATO procurement catalog. Northrop Grumman and Axon Enterprise from the United States, Quantum Systems from Germany, and OSL from the United Kingdom are the other four parties to the latest agreement of the international military alliance.
Faster procurement of listed items
Expanding on the Framework Contract for Counter-Unmanned Aircraft Systems (C-UAS), which is a part of Drone Edge Marketplace under NATO’s Rapid Adoption Action Plan, the company said it has been designed to shorten procurement cycles through a catalog of preselected systems, allowing the allied countries to buy or lease the defense system.
”This new procurement model gives Allies speed and agility against rapidly evolving threats,” the company said.
Without sharing many details about the specifics of the weapon system, the company said that the six lots cover area defense and border protection. “It is the only supplier selected for area defense across all three mobility levels: static, transportable, and on-the-move,” the company said in a statement.
The said category spans different military requirements, which include protecting munition depots and air bases, and could expand to deploying temporary defensive positions or assisting military units near the conflict areas.
More from Military
See All
Battle-tested “kill systems”
The French company highlighted that its “kill systems” are battle-tested, with its software drawing on the operational data collected in Ukraine and the Gulf.
”Its systems are built against the threat, not just tested against it,” it said.
The company has deployed its counter-drone technologies in Ukraine since 2024, where it has received direct feedback from deployed units operating against aerial threats such as Shahed-type one-way attack drones and loitering munitions.
”A counter-drone system has to work end-to-end, from detecting a threat to intercepting it. We built Alta Ares around that requirement, with software informed by battlefield data from Ukraine,” said Hadrien Canter, CEO and founder of Alta Ares.
The interceptor technologies developed by the company include Pixel Lock, a computer-vision solution designed for target detection and tracking, and Cyclop C2, which supports interceptor guidance using information provided by connected sensors and command systems. The other interceptor weapon system built by the French startup is the X-Lock interceptor with a stated range of over 9 miles (15 kilometers) and a maximum speed of nearly 200 miles per hour (310 km/hr). Black Bird, a turbojet-powered interceptor project, doubles the announced speed, 435 mph (700 km/hr), and range, 19 miles (30 km), of the X-Lock interceptor, is also part of the company’s ammunition against the growing drone threats in modern warfare.
The company has not mentioned which of these configurations made it to the NATO framework.
However, following the selection, the company is boosting production with its industrial partners and establishing dedicated teams to support contract implementation.
”We are committed to making affordable, next-generation air defense capabilities available at the scale Allied countries need,” Canter added.
For larger orders, the company is considering production arrangements in customer countries while expanding its European supply chain.

india-deep-tech-aa8a7cd572.headline: Gujarat Startup Funding Signals a Shift Towards Deep-Tech Growth
india-deep-tech-aa8a7cd572.fulltext:
Gujarat startup funding has crossed Rs 287 crore across six ventures in four months, but the more important signal is where that capital is going. The companies are working on hydrogen-powered drones, space imaging, edge artificial intelligence for vehicle safety, lunar mobility, climate-risk insurance and specialised travel platforms. Together, they suggest that the state’s startup economy is moving beyond software-led growth towards technologies that interact directly with transport, industrial systems, public safety, resilience and physical infrastructure.
The funding figures, reported by the Times of India, span ventures at very different stages. The largest round went to Ahmedabad-headquartered insurtech company In Risk Labs, which raised $27 million, or about Rs 255.8 crore, in a Series A round co-led by Bessemer Venture Partners and Northpoint Capital. At the other end of the scale, Cellegant Energy Systems raised Rs 2.6 crore to develop hybrid hydrogen fuel-cell electric drivetrain systems for drones and unmanned aerial vehicles.
The combined amount is therefore not a uniform measure of startup performance. It reflects one substantial insurance-technology round alongside smaller seed and pre-seed investments in research-intensive companies. Yet the composition of the portfolio matters. Five of the six ventures are developing or applying specialised technology in areas where hardware, data, regulation and operational reliability are as important as software.
That distinction is significant for Gujarat’s urban and industrial economy. A software platform can often scale through digital distribution. A hydrogen drivetrain, space imaging sensor, rider-assistance system or lunar mobility platform must move through testing, engineering, manufacturing partnerships, institutional procurement and, in several cases, safety or regulatory processes. The funding announced in the report is consequently an indicator of attempts to build capabilities that connect laboratories and engineering teams to real-world systems.
The strongest example is Cellegant Energy Systems, founded by IIT Gandhinagar professor Dr Atul Bhargav. The company is developing indigenous hybrid hydrogen fuel-cell electric drivetrain systems intended to extend the endurance of drones and other unmanned aerial vehicles. The same technology, according to the report, may also be used in marine and underwater vehicles, autonomous vehicles, quadruped robots and stationary power systems.
Cellegant plans to advance its 35-kg drone programme from technology readiness level three to level six within six to 12 months. That proposed movement is important because it represents a shift from an early demonstration stage towards a system that is closer to operational validation. The report does not establish whether the target will be achieved, but it does show the type of development hurdle facing deep-tech companies: capital must finance a progression from technical concept to a reliable product that can function outside a controlled laboratory environment.
## Gujarat startup funding and the hardware challenge
The presence of GVFL Prarambh Fund Trust, Co Create Aarambh and the incubator at IIT Gandhinagar in Cellegant’s round also illustrates the layered financing often required by early-stage technology ventures. University-linked incubation can support the earliest phase, while seed funds can help companies build prototypes, recruit technical teams and conduct testing. The report identifies these institutions as investors in the company, but it does not provide a complete account of public funding, procurement support or later-stage capital available to such ventures.
GVFL also led a Rs 3.7 crore seed round in Ahmedabad-based Spectra Gaze Systems and invested Rs 3 crore in Edgeverse India. Spectra Gaze, founded by former Isro scientist Arup Banerjee, develops imaging sensors for the space and defence sectors. Its clients include Isro, PRL and Kaynes Technology, and it is developing an image sensor for Isro’s next-generation HRSAT programme in collaboration with AMETEK.
This case points to a different route to scale. Instead of creating a consumer-facing product, Spectra Gaze is working within a network of institutional and industrial users. Space and defence technologies typically require specialised components, long development cycles and high confidence in performance. A company’s ability to participate in such programmes depends not only on its own engineering capacity but also on access to anchor institutions and industrial partners.
Edgeverse India is applying edge AI, cameras and radar to vehicle safety. Its products include rider-assistance systems for two-wheelers and driver-monitoring solutions for commercial vehicles. These applications have a direct mobility and road-safety relevance because they are designed to process information close to the vehicle rather than rely entirely on remote data processing.
GVFL managing director Mihir Joshi said advances in hardware, semiconductor availability and edge AI are allowing systems to process large volumes of data and make decisions in real time. His statement identifies the technological foundation behind several of the investments, but it does not provide performance results, deployment numbers or evidence of adoption by vehicle manufacturers or transport operators. Those details will determine whether the technology moves beyond development into measurable safety outcomes.
The urban importance of these ventures lies in that gap between technical possibility and system-wide use. A rider-assistance device has value only when it works reliably in mixed traffic, different weather conditions and varied road environments. A driver-monitoring system becomes consequential when it is integrated into fleet operations and when its alerts lead to safer behaviour. The funding creates capacity for development, but the report does not yet establish the scale of deployment or the effect on road crashes.
## From lunar mobility to climate-risk insurance
Ahmedabad-based Cosmochute has raised $1.5 million, or around Rs 14.2 crore, in a pre-seed round led by Prosus Ventures. The company is developing LEAP, a modular lunar mobility platform intended to transport and deploy payloads on the Moon. The funds will be used for platform development, team expansion and commercialisation.
Cosmochute sits at the most specialised end of the group. Its immediate product is not an urban service, but the company’s inclusion in the funding pattern shows how Gujarat-linked ventures are entering high-technology markets where mobility, robotics and remote operations overlap. The available information does not establish a commercial deployment date or identify customers for LEAP. What it does establish is that investors are backing the platform at a pre-seed stage, before the company has reached the commercialisation phase described in its plans.
In Risk Labs represents a more immediate connection to the risks faced by cities, businesses and infrastructure operators. The company plans to expand its underwriting, actuarial, catastrophe modelling and AI capabilities, while widening coverage across climate risks, marine cargo and motor insurance. It also plans to develop parametric and structured reinsurance offerings, with part of the funding supporting its subsidiary EarthRe.
Insurance technology does not build a flood barrier, protect a warehouse or repair a damaged road. It can, however, influence how risks are measured, priced and transferred. Catastrophe modelling and climate-risk coverage become increasingly relevant when extreme events affect property, transport networks, supply chains and municipal services. The report does not quantify the company’s existing coverage, claims performance or exposure to specific climate events, so the practical scale of its impact remains unestablished.
The funding nevertheless places risk intelligence alongside hardware and mobility technologies in the state’s startup landscape. That combination is notable because urban resilience depends on both physical systems and financial mechanisms. Sensors and models can identify risks; insurance and reinsurance products can determine how losses are absorbed. The companies in this funding set operate at different points in that chain, although the supplied evidence does not show that they are working together.
## What the funding pattern reveals
The sixth company, travel-tech venture Bucketlistt.com, raised Rs 7.6 crore in seed funding with support from i Hub Gujarat. The platform connects travellers with verified experiences and helps operators reach a wider customer base. It plans to strengthen its platform, expand its operator network and enter new destinations across India.
Bucketlistt.com is more closely associated with services and local economic activity than with deep technology. Its relevance to the broader picture is that the funding group is not exclusively focused on laboratories or industrial systems. It also includes a platform attempting to organise fragmented tourism supply, verify experiences and connect smaller operators with demand.
Hiranmay Mahanta, chief executive officer of i Hub Gujarat, said the organisation initially supported the venture with a Rs 10 lakh grant and that the founder had raised up to Rs 7 crore within two years. He described adventure tourism as a growth opportunity as travel moves towards mass customisation. The reported progression from an early grant to later private funding illustrates the role incubators can play in helping a venture reach investors, although the report does not provide comparable outcomes for other companies supported by the organisation.
Taken together, the six fundraises point to three features of Gujarat’s current startup economy. First, the state is producing or attracting ventures built around specialised engineering and applied intelligence, rather than only general-purpose digital services. Second, institutional links are visible: IIT Gandhinagar, Isro, PRL, Kaynes Technology, AMETEK, GVFL and i Hub Gujarat appear in the reported company histories or funding rounds. Third, the ventures face different routes to scale, ranging from government-linked technology programmes and industrial clients to consumer platforms and insurance markets.
The Rs 287 crore total should therefore be read carefully. It is a snapshot of announced capital, not a measure of revenue, jobs, product adoption or public benefit. It also cannot by itself establish that Gujarat has solved the financing or commercialisation challenges faced by deep-tech startups. The funding rounds show investor interest and planned use of capital; they do not yet show final technology performance.
For cities and the built environment, the key question is whether these ventures can cross the distance between a promising system and dependable urban use. Hydrogen-powered drones could eventually support applications beyond conventional aviation, but their operating economics and safety requirements are not provided. Edge AI may improve vehicle safety, but the report contains no deployment or crash-reduction data. Climate-risk analytics may strengthen insurance markets, but its effect on resilience depends on coverage, pricing and claims. These limits are not weaknesses in the funding announcement; they are the next evidence that will be needed to assess impact.

         ASUNCION
     For years, Paraguay’s digital bank, ueno, stood out as a homegrown success story, luring roughly half the country’s people to open accounts and offering many the opportunity to hold a bank account for the very first time.
But over just five days this week, the bank collapsed, freezing the savings of nearly 3 million customers — in a country of 6.5 million people — and triggering the country’s deepest political crisis in more than a decade.
On Friday evening, President Santiago Peña was impeached after attempting to resign, and his vice president, Pedro Alliana, was sworn in as his replacement.
Authorities quickly arrested Peña, an economist and close ally of US President Donald Trump, and prosecutors charged him on Saturday with breach of trust and administration for personal gain. A judge ordered him held in pretrial detention at a military facility.
Peña has denied wrongdoing and his attorney, Ricardo Preda, told journalists that he was pleading not guilty to the charges.
The scandal has triggered public protests and sharp rebukes from the opposition.
“We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history,” said opposition Senator Rafael Filizzola on Friday. “This impeachment is a first step toward ensuring justice is served.”
Manuel Ferreira, a Paraguayan economist and former finance minister, echoed much of the public anger over the case. “This was a modern-day Bonnie and Clyde,” he said. “They didn’t rob us with a pistol, they robbed us with an app. The head of the gang was the president of the republic.”
Until March 2025, Peña had been a business partner of the group that owns ueno. After his election in 2023, he tapped ueno’s former president, Carlos Carvallo, to lead the central bank.
Carvallo resigned as central bank chief earlier this week. Prosecutors charged him on Saturday with breach of trust, producing false public documents and administration for personal gain. They sought his pretrial detention, which was approved by a judge.
Carvallo did not respond to a request for comment. It was not immediately clear if he had entered a plea in the case.
Peña’s lawyer, Preda, objected to the impeachment, saying that ousting a president during a bank resolution could itself be destabilizing.
“What sets a serious country apart is not that its banks don’t fail, but how it responds,” Preda said on Friday. “If there is one thing that undermines confidence in the financial system, it is attempting to oust the president without evidence.”
Ueno was launched in 2021 as a sleek, millennial-friendly banking app that quickly won over Paraguayans who had been underserved by brick-and-mortar institutions.
It soon became deeply embedded in Paraguay’s payments system. It paired its digital offering with physical branches, later sponsoring sports teams, businesses and events. As of June, public institutions — including Paraguay’s state pension fund — held roughly $850 million in accounts with the bank.
But in recent months, internal regulatory reports warning of excessive lending to certain companies were leaked to local media outlets ABC and Última Hora, triggering political scrutiny of the bank’s lending practices.
Following growing public pressure, Paraguay’s central bank on Tuesday put ueno into resolution — its strongest measure short of immediate liquidation — after determining that ueno had breached minimum solvency requirements, locking millions of customers temporarily out of their accounts.
The central bank said on Saturday that the equivalent of $160 million had since been paid out to nearly 1.2 million savers under the state deposit guarantee scheme.
Authorities have promised that depositors will be reimbursed and say the crisis is confined to ueno. But analysts say the damage to Paraguay’s reputation as a stable investment destination in South America may linger far longer than the bank resolution itself.
“This is the moment when Paraguay must demonstrate that its institutions are functioning,” Ferreira said.
