global-economics-4c32b92cdb.headline: From iPhones to GPUs: Redington, Ingram Micro ride the AI boom
global-economics-4c32b92cdb.fulltext:
Technology distributors Redington Ltd and Ingram Micro Holding Corp., best known for supplying iPhones and laptops to retailers and businesses, are emerging as beneficiaries of India’s artificial intelligence (AI) and data centre boom.
Demand for AI servers, chips, and other data centre infrastructure is becoming a growth driver for both companies, offering a new avenue for expansion.
While selling AI compute accounts for roughly a fifth of their revenue, it is among the fastest-growing segments for both firms. The companies get three-fifths of their business from supplying phones and laptops to retailers and businesses.
At Chennai-based Redington, the world’s eighth-largest technology distributor, management expects its technology solutions group (TSG) business to be its fastest-growing driver. This is despite the company getting almost a third of its business from reselling Apple phones and handling almost half of its offline distribution.
“So second half, we continue to see TSG being a very strong number one in terms of growth driver, followed by SSG (software solutions group),” said V S Hariharan, chief executive of Redington, during the company’s post-earnings conference call on 4 November. “So the value segments will be good for the second half. Typically, they've always been strong in the second half and the CPU-GPU migration as well as the SSG work will drive that.”
The TSG arm sells networking, servers, storage, power and collaboration equipment to clients. This makes up a little less than a fifth of the company’s revenue. On the other hand, the software solutions arm comprises cloud, software licensing, professional services and cybersecurity solutions. This division also makes up less than a fifth. Together, both arms make up a third of the company’s business.
Redington ended the second quarter with ₹430 billion ($4.5 billion), up 23% sequentially. This makes it a little bigger than HCL Technologies, which is the country’s third-largest tech services firm.
In the first half of the fiscal year alone, the company’s software and technology solutions business jumped 71% and 45%, respectively, compared to the company’s overall growth of 41%.
The management stated that “AI servers, the GPUs, with richer configurations and dramatically higher ASPs (average selling prices), in many cases 4x, are driving the growth. Large deals exceeded ₹3,800 crores and accounted for roughly 9% of the Group's revenue. A good chunk of the large deals in India came from data centers.”
The management said it plans to capitalize on the data centre demand through local business houses setting up shop in the country.
Redington management’s commentary comes after a larger supplier first threw light on data centre driving growth.
iPhones to AI servers
“AI is driving a lot of new solutions, new projects across cybersecurity, data center, cloud, networking, even AI PCs (personal computers). So AI is driving a lot of growth in India,” said Flavio Moraes Junior, chief country executive of Ingram Micro India, during a conversation with Mint on 24 September.
California-based Ingram Micro ended last year with $52.6 billion in revenue, up 9.5% from the year-ago period, reversing a decline in 2024. Its India business grew at a similar pace, according to its financials. India is the company’s second-largest market and accounted for about a tenth of the company's 2025 revenue, or $5 billion.
While the company does not disclose revenue from data centres, it discloses revenue from its ‘advanced solutions’ business, where the company sells servers, storage and networking devices, IT services and cybersecurity solutions, power and cooling, as well as GPU and AI-infrastructure products.
The management acknowledged that this segment was the company’s fastest-growing business segment last quarter. To be sure, the company does not individually share revenue from its ‘advanced solutions’ business.
“I think of different investment cycles that are playing out right now. In the enterprise, the AI data centers, we continue to talk about, infrastructure modernization, everything wrapped with security. And our partners are telling us they're bullish right now near-term with large pipelines in data center networking and compute,” said Paul Bay, CEO of Ingram Micro, during the company’s post-earnings analyst call on 30 October.
“The global ICT market has entered an accelerated investment cycle, led by AI infrastructure, cloud computing, software and next-generation devices,” said Motilal Oswal Financial Services analysts Chirag Kachhadiya and Sahil Satra, in a note earlier this month. “Data centre systems and infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) are emerging as the fastest-growing segments as hyperscalers and enterprises scale up their computing capacity to support AI workloads.”
According to Motilal Oswal Financial Services, the country’s installed data centre capacity currently stands at approximately 1.3GW, with developers announcing an additional 7.1GW of capacity over the next four years.

india-e076f6b4eb.headline: Microsoft launches 4th cloud region in India, bets big on AI infrastructure growth
india-e076f6b4eb.fulltext:
Microsoft has launched its fourth cloud region in India in Hyderabad, expanding its cloud and artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure footprint as the country gears up for a major increase in data centre capacity and enterprise AI adoption.
The newly launched India South Central cloud region in Hyderabad joins Microsoft’s existing cloud regions in Pune, Chennai and Mumbai, giving the technology giant its largest hyperscale cloud infrastructure presence in the country.
The launch forms part of Microsoft’s previously announced $20.5-billion investment commitment in India, aimed at strengthening cloud capabilities, AI infrastructure, skilling initiatives and operational expansion.
Speaking at the launch, Microsoft India and South Asia President Puneet Chandok said India is at a pivotal moment in its digital transformation journey, with the country emerging as one of the world’s largest generators of data.
According to Chandok, India now generates nearly 20 per cent of the world’s data but accounts for only about 3 per cent of global data centre capacity.
“20 per cent of the world’s data is being generated by India, but only 3 per cent of the world’s data centre capacity sits in our country,” Chandok said.
“Between these two numbers sits the largest opportunity of the decade for India,” he added.
India currently has about 2 gigawatts (GW) of data centre capacity, a figure Chandok expects to increase to between 12 GW and 14 GW by 2035. He said the rapid expansion would be necessary as businesses, government departments and institutions move beyond AI experimentation and begin deploying AI applications at scale.
Chandok emphasised that demand for AI services is already strong and that the key challenge is building sufficient infrastructure to support future growth.
“The digital scale that we are building requires physical scale, and that is the national imperative for all of us,” he mentioned.

world-752bfb0c9b.headline: Cop31 must deliver climate progress that people can see is real, host says
world-752bfb0c9b.fulltext:
The Cop31 summit must produce progress, “a tangible outcome ... that people can see is real”, its host has said as scores of world leaders and representatives of close to 190 countries gather in Turkey for the UN climate talks.
The high-stakes meeting begins on Monday, as countries around the world grapple with the strongest El Niño weather system on record, supercharged by fossil fuels, which is set to take hundreds of thousands of lives and cause damage costing trillions of dollars.
Friction is expected between the rich and poor worlds over who pays for the impacts of the climate crisis, and the slow pace of cutting greenhouse gas emissions. Temperatures have broken records this year, surpassing the limit of 1.5C above preindustrial levels aimed for in the 2015 Paris climate agreement.
Adão Soares Barbosa, the chair of the Least Developed Countries, a negotiating group of 44 nations, said: “Keeping 1.5C within reach by minimising the duration and magnitude of the overshoot, delivering accessible and predictable climate finance, strengthening adaptation, and addressing loss and damage [caused to poor countries by extreme weather] are not political choices but matters of survival. The credibility of the Paris agreement will be measured not by promises made, but by commitments fulfilled, and lives protected in vulnerable countries.”
Unusually, the talks will have dual hosts: they will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya but the formal negotiations will be presided over by Australia, following a compromise reached last year over their competing bids.
Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister and president of negotiations for Cop31, told the Guardian in an interview: “We need a tangible outcome focused on implementation [of emissions cuts and finance] that people can see is real. We need progress, it needs to be a step forward on previous Cops.”
Australia also wants a “strong, ambitious outcome” to raise the plight of low-lying countries in the Pacific region for whom the climate crisis poses an existential threat. “We need to finally elevate some of the issues so important to our Pacific family,” Bowen said. “[Only] 0.2% of the world’s available climate finance goes to small island developing states for adaptation, for countries whose very existence is at stake.”
But climate advocates and more than 500 scientists in Australia said Australia must stop approving coalmines and gas projects if it wanted to escape the charge of hypocrisy.
The summit will have a notable absentee, with the US refusing to send a delegation for the second year in a row. The Trump administration wants no part of “extremist climate policies” embraced by other countries, according to a White House spokesperson.
Donald Trump expressed glee shortly before the US midterm elections about the huge profits made by oil and gas companies due to the Iran war, which he started and has caused an increase in living costs around the world. “I don’t give a damn,” the president said at a recent rally in Georgia. “I’m going to say it: we’re making a frickin’ fortune.”
However, a group of 20 Democratic members of Congress have made the trip to Antalya, buoyed by their party’s stunning success in the US midterms last week that will enable them to stymie Trump’s attempts to dismantle pollution rules and withhold financial support for clean energy.
Developing countries and civil society will seek to put climate finance and justice at the heart of the Cop31 talks. Rukiya Khamis, the east Africa programme manager at the 350.org campaigning group, said: “Across east Africa, people are facing the devastating impacts of a climate crisis they did not cause. From prolonged droughts to destructive floods, we are losing homes, livelihoods and access to food and water. Yet the money needed to respond to these impacts remains out of reach for many of the countries and communities most affected. It is fundamentally unjust that those least responsible are being left to carry the greatest costs.”
This summer more than 50,000 people died in Europe due to heatwaves, severe wildfire smoke shrouded swathes of North America and a glacier collapse in Nepal triggered a landslide that caused more than 1,500 deaths, while the El Niño weather event, described as “staggering” by scientists and still to reach its peak, is gathering strength.
However, while the pace of progress on cutting global emissions has been slow, the Iran war has spurred many countries to see fossil fuels as expensive and vulnerable to shocks, while renewables continue to plummet in price.
Simon Stiell, the UN’s climate chief, said before the talks: “Climate impacts hit every population and every economy harder each year. [But] almost every major economy, and many medium-sized and smaller economies, now see climate action as a central driver of economic growth, jobs, and affordable and secure energy.”
Cop host Turkey also wants more countries to switch to electric technologies, such as electric vehicles and heat pumps, as these are many times more efficient than their fossil fuel counterparts. A target for 35% of global final energy to come from electricity by 2035 will be on the table, but faces opposition from some.
Both presidency countries rely heavily on fossil fuels. Australia is one of the world’s leading exporters of coal and liquefied natural gas. The centre-left Labor government has targets to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, and have more than 80% of its electricity generated by solar and wind by 2030, but is off track to meet them.
Labor also faces a political threat from the resurgent rightwing One Nation party, which dismisses climate science. One Nation and the Liberal and National party coalition want to scrap the net zero goal.
The UK energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: “This summer, we all felt it: climate change is here, in Britain, now. No country can tackle it alone, which is why Cop31 matters. The answer to high bills and climate change is the same – more clean, homegrown power, creating good jobs and warmer homes. Cop31 is about Britain’s national interest.”

work-careers-4e18535211.headline: Indian CEOs plan AI-driven workforce cuts even as hiring rises: KPMG
work-careers-4e18535211.fulltext:
KPMG's 2026 CEO Outlook finds 52 per cent of Indian business leaders planning workforce cuts in some areas, even as 92 per cent expect overall headcount to grow over three years.
KPMG's twelfth annual CEO Outlook surveyed 1,400 CEOs across 12 markets between 11 August and 21 September 2026. (Photo/File)
More than half of Indian chief executive officers are planning workforce reductions in some business areas even as they expect overall hiring to increase, according to KPMG‘s 2026 India CEO Outlook released in October. The survey of 125 Indian CEOs found that companies are simultaneously investing in artificial intelligence, reassessing existing roles and recruiting people with new technological skills.
The report found that 78 per cent of Indian CEOs consider AI a top investment priority, broadly matching the global figure of 79 per cent. However, 52 per cent of Indian respondents are planning workforce cuts in certain areas, up from 50 per cent in 2025, even as 92 per cent expect their organisations’ total headcount to grow over the next three years.
KPMG’s twelfth annual CEO Outlook surveyed 1,400 CEOs across 12 markets between 11 August and 21 September 2026. All respondents lead companies with annual revenues exceeding $500 million.
The findings point to a restructuring of work rather than net job losses. About 86 per cent of Indian CEOs are reviewing the skills required for entry-level positions, compared with 76 per cent globally. The proportion prioritising retention and retraining of high-potential employees rose to 87 per cent from 70 per cent last year.
Business confidence remains high. About 87 per cent of Indian CEOs expressed confidence in their companies’ growth prospects over the next three years, up from 83 per cent in 2025. Globally, confidence increased to 84 per cent from 79 per cent.
The survey found that 62 per cent of Indian CEOs expect to allocate between 11 and 20 per cent of their budgets to AI over the next 12 months. About 70 per cent expect returns on these investments within one to three years.
Nearly 97 per cent of Indian respondents said their companies could keep pace with AI developments and their implications for business operations. However, confidence in understanding the technology’s wider business implications was lower, with 75 per cent of Indian CEOs saying their leadership teams understood how AI would disrupt existing business models.
Adoption of agentic AI, which refers to software systems that can execute tasks and workflows with varying degrees of autonomy rather than simply responding to prompts, is also gaining attention. According to the survey, 46 per cent of Indian CEOs said agentic AI was already having a significant or transformational impact on their organisations, compared with 55 per cent globally.
Purushothaman KG, partner and head of AI and technology transformation at KPMG in India, said the next phase of AI would be defined by an “organisation’s ability to translate investment into measurable value”. This would require companies to strengthen governance, data infrastructure, workforce capabilities and cybersecurity, he said.
The survey identified several barriers to enterprise-wide AI implementation. Ethical challenges emerged as the leading concern, cited by 64 per cent of Indian CEOs compared with 57 per cent globally.
Regulatory complexity was another significant issue. About 53 per cent of Indian respondents identified inconsistent regional AI regulations as an implementation challenge, substantially higher than the global figure of 41 per cent. Additionally, 70 per cent of Indian CEOs said the pace of AI regulation could impede organisational success.
Data sovereignty requirements present challenges for 50 per cent of respondents in both India and the global sample. Implementation costs remain a concern for 51 per cent of Indian respondents, while 53 per cent identified difficulties integrating AI with existing security infrastructure.
Cybersecurity and data security emerged as the leading threats to business growth, cited by 38 per cent of Indian CEOs. Global economic uncertainty and geopolitical instability followed, each identified by 28 per cent of respondents.
In response, 49 per cent of Indian CEOs are increasing investment in cybersecurity and digital-risk resilience, compared with 45 per cent globally. Another 34 per cent are prioritising AI integration across operations, while 33 per cent are directing additional investment towards regulatory compliance.
About 97 per cent of Indian CEOs expressed concern about fraud detection and prevention. Identity theft and data privacy concerned 96 per cent of Indian respondents, while 87 per cent expressed concern about vulnerability to cyberattacks.
The report identified additional security risks arising from agentic AI deployment, including expanded attack surfaces and new identity and access management requirements.
Mohit Bahl, partner and head of risk and integrity advisory, KPMG in India, said risk management was evolving from an operational necessity into a strategic leadership imperative. Boards and executive teams should consider integrating risk management, resilience and governance more closely with investment and growth decisions, he said.
Talent availability remains a significant concern for Indian businesses. About 54 per cent of CEOs identified attracting and retaining employees as a major workforce challenge, followed by skills gaps at 53 per cent and AI-related employee training at 51 per cent.
Indian businesses are adopting different approaches to workforce preparation. About 48 per cent of CEOs are prioritising organisation-wide AI education, while 44 per cent are focusing on role-specific training. Nearly 79 per cent said AI was changing how their organisations train and develop staff.
On economic outlook, confidence in India’s growth prospects increased to 73 per cent from 71 per cent in 2025. Advancing digitisation and connectivity was the leading operational priority for 26 per cent of Indian CEOs, compared with 20 per cent globally.
The survey found 62 per cent of Indian CEOs expect to allocate between 11 and 20 per cent of their budgets to AI over the next 12 months, with 70 per cent expecting returns within one to three years.

other-interests-6c46f2aa79.headline: Antipersonnel mines have returned in Ukraine and now threaten the world
other-interests-6c46f2aa79.fulltext:
Antipersonnel (AP) mines seemed to be on the way out in 1997, when 122 countries signed the Ottawa Treaty to ban them. But in 2026, such mines are making a comeback.
“These things are both cheap to produce and offer a level of sophistication that actors couldn’t hope to reproduce for a hundred times the price only a few years ago,” says Seán Moorhouse, an explosive ordnance disposal consultant.
AP mines come in two forms. Blast mines, weighing 100 grams or less, are typically scattered by aircraft. Activated by pressure, blast mines are designed to maim. Larger fragmentation mines, laid by combat engineers, have tripwires and spray lethal fragments in all directions.
Advertisement
Moorhouse notes that three technologies have enabled the resurgence of AP mines in Ukraine: 3D printing, microcontrollers and drone delivery.
3D printing enables any frontline unit to produce its own mines. Different shapes, sizes and colours proliferate, making mines harder to spot. Some, like the curved, green Caterpillar, blend in with vegetation. Urban mines, meanwhile, may look like pieces of brick or concrete.
Fragmentation mines can be triggered by microcontrollers connected to sensors rather than tripwires. In Ukraine, the most common type, nicknamed Jonik (“little soldier”), is magnetic and sensitive enough to be set off by a rifle carried nearby. Doppler microwave sensors detect movement; others sense body heat or vibration. A new variety is triggered by the approach of any Bluetooth device.
Drone delivery of both blast and fragmentation types has been transformational. Drones slip far behind the lines to place mines precisely on tracks and paths, or around trenches, giving a greater chance of finding a victim than random scattering. Human rights organisations and a UN commission have reported that Russian forces are using drones to drop AP mines to target civilians in the city of Kherson.
The combination of these technologies makes mines both deadlier and more accessible. “The triad of drone delivery, 3D printing and microcontrollers will proliferate worldwide,” predicts Moorhouse.
Networks of soldiers and volunteer groups produce mines in garage workshops in Ukraine and Russia. The technology is easy to replicate.
“These simple devices can be rapidly produced by any group with access to explosives, enabling a significant expansion of mine warfare,” says Roy Gardiner at the non-profit group Defense Tech for Ukraine.
AP mines present a threat to civilians for decades after a conflict. When the Ottawa Treaty was signed, this lasting danger outweighed any military value. The calculus seems to have changed. Ukraine suspended its implementation of the treaty, and others have also changed their minds.
“Now we see five countries pulling out of the Ottawa Treaty [Poland, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia], which suggests that mines have some utility,” says Moorhouse.
He says demining agencies need to act urgently to adapt to the challenges of new AP mines and update their training and awareness programmes. Technology may mitigate the problem, with AI-enabled drones beginning to play a role in mine detection and disposal. But Moorhouse warns the risk from AP mines is growing rather than shrinking, and many states and non-state actors are likely to adopt these cheap, accessible and effective weapons, despite the human cost.

ai-bc55171edc.headline: Nvidia will investigate CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with possible Chinese spy
ai-bc55171edc.fulltext:
Nvidia’s board of directors announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation.
Nvidia also published a message that Huang sent to the company admitting that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed (though he didn’t mention her by name). A memo circulating among U.S. policymakers earlier this year claimed that Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Jensen Huang wrote. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Huang added that he’d “fallen short” of his responsibility to the company.
“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” he said.
As the AI race between the United States and China heats up, chips, especially Nvidia’s chips, have been a major focus. Huang also seems to have a close relationship with President Donald Trump, who’s been a cheerleader of the AI (or “superintelligence”) industry.
In its announcement, Nvidia’s board said that it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or company secrets were compromised. It also said that Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” and that the board has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”
The investigation will be conducted by independent directors working with outside legal counsel.
In response to earlier reports about the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, Nvidia had said that the pair’s interactions were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with customers.
Other companies involved in the AI boom have warned employees to be wary of possible spies, including those offering sex or romance.

world-2b527a5d8a.headline: Nvidia opens investigation after report CEO Jensen Huang was target of foreign intelligence
world-2b527a5d8a.fulltext:
Nvidia said on Sunday it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.
The New York Times reported in October that Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence that Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”
Trump also brushed off a question about whether he now regrets not acting on the intelligence when he was briefed on it, and suggested that he would be happy to take Huang with him on a trip to Asia next week. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody. But, you know, so does everybody else.”
Republican lawmakers have expressed more alarm, asking Huang to give the Houseforeign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his relationship withAlice Huang or Huang Le, an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed, who is of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her.
Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
The company’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.
“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”
Huang fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added.
Axios reported on Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full responsibility for his actions.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did,” Huang said in the draft email also seen by Reuters.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report.
The Times reported on Sunday that a memo drafted by US secretary of state Marco Rubio circulated among top policymakers in the Trump administration last spring, citing intelligence that the businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive was a spy for China’s ministry of state security. Despite those concerns, Huang was invited to join Trump’s delegation when he traveled to China in May. Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, were also invited to a state dinner at the White House in September for Xi Jinping and seated at the top table with Trump and China’s president.
Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom, placing Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
However, national security concerns have prompted strict US export controls, effectively barring the company from selling its top-tier processors to customers in China.
US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as a rationale for the restrictions. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Alice Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.
A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.
Nick Robins-Early and Blake Montgomery contributed reporting

world-537b0cc6a7.headline: US chipmaker Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang over affair

US chipmaker Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang over affair
Huang has confirmed he had been having an affair with a woman accused of spying for China.
United States-based chipmaker Nvidia is investigating its chief executive officer, billionaire Jensen Huang, after he confirmed he had an intimate relationship with a woman accused of working for Chinese intelligence.
In an announcement on Sunday, Nvidia said the probe would be conducted by a “committee of independent directors” with outside counsel.
“While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” Nvidia’s board of directors said.
It said the board continued to have “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team”. Huang will continue to lead Nvidia during the probe.
The investigation follows a report in The New York Times last month that Jensen may have been the target of a Chinese espionage plot.
China and the US have been in competition to dominate key tech sectors like artificial intelligence (AI).
Amid the AI boom, Nvidia has seen demand for its chips and programming interfaces explode, resulting in the company being valued in the trillions of dollars.
For years, the US has sought to restrict the export of advanced chips to China, fearing the Asian superpower could gain an edge over its technology and military sectors.
But on October 29, The New York Times said it had obtained exclusive information that a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, or Huang Le, sought to cultivate close ties with Jensen Huang in an effort to glean information about Nvidia’s technology.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington, DC, has denied any allegations of spying in the case.
The New York Times also reported that Alice Huang’s employer, Megaspeed, had become one of Nvidia’s largest buyers, purchasing some $4.8bn in equipment from the US firm.
Jensen Huang’s ties to Alice Huang, who is of no relation, spurred fierce bipartisan backlash in the US Congress in the aftermath of the report.
“For months, bipartisan members of Congress have raised concerns about NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips going to China,” Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote in a statement.
“NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang and NVIDIA’s board owe Congress answers. And we need to pass bipartisan legislation we have ready to stop advanced American technology from going to China.”
Republican lawmakers in the House of Representatives also called on Huang to appear and testify before Congress about the affair on November 18.
“It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” Republicans John Moolenaar, Brian Mast and Rick Crawford said in a statement.
In an email to Nvidia staff on Sunday, Huang had admitted to having an extramarital relationship.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did,” Huang said.
Nvidia has grown rapidly in recent years with the rise of AI, producing chips for large language models developed by companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google.
Huang has also been closely working with US President Donald Trump since the Republican leader returned to office in 2025.
In August of that year, the Trump administration announced it would take a 15 percent cut of certain Nvidia chip sales to China.
Trump reportedly bought as much as $1.6m in Nvidia stock and sold about $1m in August, ahead of November’s midterm elections.
After the midterm races last Tuesday, stocks for AI-related companies, including Nvidia, tumbled in reaction to widespread Republican losses.
Trump has pushed back against calls to regulate AI companies, but many Democrats during the midterms campaigned on placing restrictions on the companies, including on the construction of data centres.
Nvidia lost $450bn in market value in a single trading day last week, but it rebounded on Friday, regaining 4 percent of its losses.
When asked by reporters if Huang would accompany him to November’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China, Trump was noncommittal.
“I don’t know, but I’d certainly take him,” Trump replied from the tarmac in West Palm Beach, Florida. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong. He dealt with somebody, but so does everybody else.”
He added that Huang was a “fine person” and has done an “amazing job for our country”.
“I think he’s an honourable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it,” Trump said of the speculation about Huang’s behaviour.

global-economics-49a21f8688.headline: Global AI sell-off turns into India's gain as FPIs pump ₹46,000 crore in 5 sessions; will the buying spree sustain?
global-economics-49a21f8688.fulltext:
A KsheerasagarPublished8 Nov 2026, 05:01 PM IST It appears that foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have changed their bearish stance towards the Indian stock market, buying domestic equities aggressively last week and pouring in a massive ₹45,970 crore in just five trading sessions. This marks a strong turnaround after foreign investors remained net sellers for two consecutive months. The shift in sentiment boosted the Nifty 50 by 8.6% during the week, marking its strongest weekly performance since February 2021. The rally also helped the index pare its year-to-date losses to 4.21%. At its lowest point this year, the index had fallen nearly 15% but has since recovered close to 13% from its yearly low. In addition to equities, the inflows have also strengthened the Indian rupee, which had suffered multiple record lows this year. The currency climbed 0.6% to 93.91 against the US dollar, its strongest level since April. The shift in sentiment towards Asia's third-largest economy comes amid a correction in global AI-linked stocks. Concerns over a potential move by the US Congress, led by Democrats, to impose restrictions on the massive expansion of data centres in the US triggered a sell-off in previously favoured chip and memory stocks across Asia. In addition, the sharp retreat in crude oil prices has eased inflation concerns, particularly as India remains heavily dependent on oil imports. An improving earnings outlook has further enhanced the appeal of Indian equities among foreign investors. India's relatively low exposure to the AI trade had previously left its stocks among Asia's worst performers. However, as the once high-flying trade begins to unravel, that weakness has quickly turned into an advantage. Dheeraj Gaur, Chief Investment Strategy Officer at Choice Wealth, said three factors came together to drive the sharp rally in Indian equities. First, politics and oil: the US midterm results were read as raising the odds of a de-escalation in the US–Iran conflict, and Brent fell about 13% to roughly $98 – its steepest weekly drop since the start of Covid. Cheaper oil is the single biggest relief for India’s inflation, current account and rupee, and the rupee strengthened to about 93.90 per dollar from around 95.4 a week ago. Second, the AI trade cracked. A tech rout on Thursday took the Nasdaq down 5.5% and the S&P 500 4.4%, after weak Qualcomm results and worries about slowing AI infrastructure spending, and Korea and Japan fell about 6% on Friday. Global funds have been rotating out of AI-linked names into markets like India, which has little AI exposure – Indian IT stocks even rose. Third, India simply looked cheap after a poor year, with earnings holding up. Looking ahead, Dheeraj Gaur, said several factors will determine the direction of FPI flows. The US Consumer Price Index (CPI) data due on Tuesday, November 10, will be closely watched. With a December rate hike nearly priced in, a hotter-than-expected inflation reading could push bond yields and the US dollar higher. Gaur also highlighted crude oil prices and developments in the Gulf region as key factors to watch, particularly whether Brent crude sustains below the $100-a-barrel mark or the de-escalation narrative begins to lose momentum. In addition, commentary from Federal Reserve officials and movements in US bond yields will be closely monitored following the latest jobs report, as any hawkish messaging around a December rate hike could influence global fund flows. Nov 5 (Reuters) - Zipline said on Thursday it has raised $1.5 billion in its latest funding round, valuing the US drone delivery startup at $21.5 billion post-money, nearly tripling its valuation in about 10 months.
The funding comes as competition in drone delivery intensifies, with companies expanding their delivery networks, although regulatory approvals and community concerns over noise and safety remain barriers to broader adoption.
The round was led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global and drew participation from Uber, Tiger Global and J.P. Morgan, among others.
The company plans to use the funding to expand its US manufacturing capacity, hire more workers and develop a nationwide drone delivery network.
Chief Executive Keller Cliffton told Reuters in an interview that Zipline had to develop much of its technology and manufacturing operation itself because there was no established drone-delivery supply chain to draw from.
"None of our customers care about drones. They care about teleportation, and so that meant that we had to do everything necessary on the back end to build this."
Cliffton said regulatory restrictions initially kept Zipline from launching commercially in its home market, prompting the company to begin operations overseas.?
"For the first 10 years from when we built the company, operating beyond visual line of sight was illegal in the US," he added. "It's the reason that we launched outside the US for the first eight years of our commercial operations."
Zipline, which operates across four continents, was valued at $7.6 billion when it raised $600 million earlier this year.
In August, the company partnered with Uber to bring autonomous drone delivery to Uber Eats customers, with the ride-hailing giant also taking a strategic stake at an undisclosed valuation.
Amazon, meanwhile, also plans to expand its drone-delivery service from 11 locations to about 500 US locales by year-end.

Other investors in the round included Valor Equity Partners, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Uber, Tiger Global, J.P. Morgan, ARK Invest and Salesforce Ventures.
The new valuation is about 2.8x Zipline’s $7.6 billion valuation in January and more than 5x the $4.2 billion figure Tech Funding News reported in May 2023.
Zipline is planning to invest in US manufacturing and hiring as it expands its nationwide drone delivery network. In January, it raised over $600 million, and in March it increased that by $200 million as part of Series H.
Investors behind the $1.5 billion round
The three lead investors are all relatively new to logistics. Paradigm, a San Francisco-based firm that has made early investments in Uniswap and Flashbots, joined the March extension to Zipline with no prior experience in logistics, according to Dealroom.
Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at Paradigm, said, “Zipline is now one of the largest autonomous robotics companies in the world, operating with scale, safety, and a magical user experience for consumers and merchants. It’s no wonder that some of the largest merchants in the world are partnering with Zipline to use their delivery network.”
WCM is a growth equity firm based in Laguna Beach, CA, which was founded in 1976. Layer Global, founded in February 2026 by Anton Levy, former co-CEO of General Atlantic, is less than a year old.
Alan Tu, portfolio manager at WCM Investment Management, noted, “Zipline has built a team and culture that has been developing cutting-edge drone delivery capabilities for over 10 years, and the market is now recognizing how transformational its technology is. Within e-commerce and food delivery, Zipline represents a generational improvement in user experience and delight.”
Anton Levy, founder & managing partner at Layer Global, added, “Zipline has already brought the future of delivery to the communities it serves. Now, the opportunity is to reach millions more. With partners like Uber and Walmart and a repeatable model for entering new markets, Zipline is well positioned to make drone delivery a mainstream part of everyday life.”
Zipline’s offerings and disclosed metrics
Rinaudo Cliffton co-founded the company in 2014 with Keenan Wyrobek, a robotics engineer who had worked on the Robot Operating System, Ryan Oksenhorn, and Will Hetzle in South San Francisco.
Zipline is based in South San Francisco and was founded in Half Moon Bay in 2014. They design their own aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software. The Platform 2 drone can hover up to 300 feet and deliver via tether, capable of carrying up to 8lbs over a 10-mile range.
Walmart and Zipline are evaluating 300 more sites under a multi-year national agreement. As of May, 66 Walmart drone stores were operating using Zipline and Alphabet’s Wing. Meanwhile, Uber wants to get to one million Zipline deliveries a day by 2029 via Uber Eats, starting in cities like Dallas and Houston.
Zipline says hundreds of businesses generate revenue through the network, and dozens of new businesses join every week. For its most established restaurant partners, Zipline’s share of delivery revenue rose from 10.8% in March to 34.9% in October. Delivery gross merchandise value has increased 26%, with 80% of that growth attributable to new Zipline orders. DroneXL notes that Zipline selected this group but doesn’t state how many restaurants were in it.
The company states its drones have logged 150 million commercial autonomous miles with zero safety incidents. Zipline also claims its medical deliveries save over 14,000 lives per year and that it is building a network in Côte d’Ivoire that will serve over 2,200 health facilities and 12 million people.
Pending regulatory changes
Zipline is now operating under Part 135 authorisations. The proposed Part 108 rule from the FAA would allow drones to fly beyond the visual line of sight as a routine operation, replacing the current waiver process.
Europe’s best-funded competitor is smaller than Zipline. Manna raised a $50 million Series B in 2026, while Flytrex, the Israeli startup, was already operating for Walmart by then.
Mordor Intelligence forecasts the delivery drone market to grow from $1.08 billion in 2025 to $4.40 billion by 2030. Zipline’s valuation is nearly five times that of the projected 2030 market size.
TFN’s European drone coverage has focused heavily on defence and cargo, with Quantum Systems’ $1.2 billion round at an $8 billion valuation in July and Dronamics’ planned Nasdaq listing at a $400 million pre-money valuation. Zipline is valued at around 2.7x Quantum Systems. That follows Fal’s $1.3 billion Series F at a $16 billion valuation on 4th November, and robotics and embodied AI were the big story in June’s funding.
Zipline says it can get an order out to a customer 19 minutes after checkout. The big question is whether the 300 Walmart sites, Uber’s one million-per-day target, and expanded manufacturing can all go ahead on a timetable that’s still very much in doubt, given the FAA and local authorities.

agritech-dc24b6af01.headline: Report flags hailstorms’ growing impact on Indian farms during pre-monsoon season
agritech-dc24b6af01.fulltext:
A farmer inspects damaged bananas after Cyclone Arnab tore through Konaseema, Andhra Pradesh, on October 28.
Hailstorms have emerged as a key factor impacting agriculture during the pre-monsoon season, a climate assessment report has flagged.
“Alongside the monsoon, the pre-monsoon season is emerging as another period of heightened risk for agriculture. Between March and May, at least 0.73 million hectares of cropped land were affected — the second-highest loss recorded during the pre-monsoon season… after 2023,” the report prepared by the Centre for Science and Environment states.
During the pre-monsoon season, lightning and storms were the most frequent extreme weather events, the report flagged. “Hailstorms, a major part of these events, occurred on 80 per cent of the days in April and May 2026, affecting 27 states and causing significant crop damage,” it added.
The CSE underlined these erratic patterns in its report on Climate India 2026: An Assessment of Extreme Weather Events. The assessment pointed out that the five-year period (2022-26) saw major changes in seasonal weather patterns.
“At least 20.6 million hectares of cropped land were affected between 2022 and 2026, with more than 82 per cent of the damage occurring in the last three years,” the report said.
“The affected area rose from 1.84 million hectares in 2022 and 1.84 million hectares in 2023 to 3.2 million hectares in 2024. In 2025, it shot up to 9.47 million hectares. In 2026, another 4.25 million hectares were affected, the second-highest figure in five years,” the report said.
“In 2026... heavy rain, floods and landslides occurred somewhere in the country on all 122 days of the monsoon season, damaging at least 3.44 million hectares of cropped land,” it added.

beyond-your-beat-c59f5aa6ae.headline: Air pollution over 50 times WHO limit in parts of Delhi as people defy ban on firecrackers on Deepavali
beyond-your-beat-c59f5aa6ae.fulltext:
As Delhiites burst firecrackers well past the 10 p.m. deadline set by the Supreme Court for Deepavali night, air pollution shot up to over 50 times World Health Organisation (WHO) limits in parts of the city, official data showed.
The level of PM2.5 (a major pollutant) in Akshardham was 760.99 micrograms per cubic meter at 11 p.m. on Sunday (November 8, 2026), as per Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) data. This is about 50.73 times the WHO permissible limit of 15 micrograms per cubic meter for a 24-hour period.
Deepavali 2026: All you need to know about Supreme Court-permitted time slots, green crackers and other directives
PM2.5 (Particulate Matter 2.5) are fine inhalable particles, which can get into lungs and bloodstream and lead to a range of respiratory and other diseases.
The level of PM2.5 in Anand Vihar was 767 micrograms per cubic meter at 11 p.m. on Sunday (November 8, 2026), as per DPCC data — This is about 51.13 times the WHO permissible limit.
The level of PM2.5 in Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium was 702 micrograms per cubic meter, as per DPCC data, which is about 46.8 times the WHO permissible limit.
The overall air quality of Delhi continued to be in the “very poor” category while many parts of the city continued to reel under “severe” air quality.
Every winter, air pollution spikes in Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.
